source.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Connor Kissane; Robert Krzyzanowski; J. Bloom; Arthur Conmy; Neel Nanda

page_placements.theme: Attention heads: monosemantic vs polysemantic roles

record.tranche_reason: The paper motivates attention-output sparse autoencoders as an alternative analysis unit partly because neurons and attention heads can be polysemantic, but it does not test the claimed neuron-pole audit or its versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports manual interpretability ratings for SAE features and polysemanticity analyses for attention heads, not neuron poles. Those adjacent results are recorded with versions ["none"]. It does not test explanations of neurons on held-out activations or automated neuron-explanation scores.
record.test_reason: The study trains sparse autoencoders on attention-layer outputs. It manually rates the resulting SAE features and attention heads, not MLP neurons or neuron poles. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited motivation (Wang et al.). The paper does not rely on it as a tool or measure it. No result bears on any version, so the study does not test the claim. 'uses_without_test'/T4 overstates the link: the paper's method does not depend on the neuron finding.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that attention-output SAEs give sparse, faithful, interpretable decompositions in models up to 2B parameters. They find the SAEs useful for interpreting heads, induction-head specialisation and the IOI circuit. They estimate at least ~90% of GPT-2 Small heads are polysemantic (14/144 monosemantic candidates). They also note that late-layer SAEs have notable reconstruction error.
record.recipe_differences: This paper trains sparse autoencoders on concatenated attention-head outputs and manually rates sampled SAE features; the claim concerns manual audits of neuron poles and explanation testing on new activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE feature interpretability percentages vary by model and layer; the authors also note that human judgments are subjective and that the SAE results depend on architecture and training quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Manual ratings of 30 sampled live attention-output SAE features per SAE found 60–97% interpretable in GPT-2 Small layers. Gemma-2B layer 6 was 66% and GELU-2L layer 1 was 83%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most sampled attention-output SAE features receive clear human descriptions, with rates varying by model and layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Of 144 GPT-2 Small attention heads, 14 (9.7%) were plausibly monosemantic from their top-10 attributed SAE features. The other 90% appear to perform at least two tasks; the authors call this a lower bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most GPT-2 Small attention heads are polysemantic by SAE-feature attribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating head 10.2 gave the largest loss increase among layer-10 heads on both digit-copying and URL-completion synthetic tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single attention heads can serve multiple unrelated tasks, confirmed without SAEs.

record.problems: The feature interpretability ratings rely on subjective judgments by paper authors, use only 30 sampled live features per SAE, and may have false positives or false negatives. The attention-head polysemanticity classification is qualitative and examines only the top ten attributed SAE features per head; the authors say it is a lower bound. The ablation plot values are not stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares; no neurons audited.
Neuron-pole shares across dense/MoE models and scale; only attention SAE features and heads are studied, in models up to 2B.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron; recursive generalization vs superposition.
Architecture/regularization/tool causes of messy neurons; vision-model interpretability shares.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model. The paper's circuit work (RDFA, IOI) uses SAE features plus error terms, not neurons.
Whether explanations from neuron activating examples predict firing elsewhere. The specificity/sensitivity checks concern SAE features only.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is adjacent to the phenomenon but concerns SAE features and attention heads, not neurons. Its only mention of neuron polysemanticity is a citation. Late-layer SAEs (layers 0 and 7–11) were insufficient for IOI circuit analysis. This bears loosely on SAE reconstruction-error concerns relevant to V5's comparison, but it is not a test of neuron-based circuits.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares of one job, two related jobs, and not-yet-understood poles.
Neuron-pole shares across other models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron interpretation, pose, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The proposed architectural, regularization, and tool causes of messy neurons, and the stated estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations of neurons derived from activating examples fail to predict neuron activation on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: Neurons come up only in the introduction's motivation, which cites prior work on polysemantic neurons. The paper's own polysemanticity analysis is about attention heads.

tranche.reason: The study measures attention heads through attention-output SAE features, not MLP neurons or neuron poles. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited motivation (intro, ref [66]). It does not test or use any version.

source_check.notes: Row R16 concerns GPT-2 Small attention heads, not neurons, so it fits no version. The text's 'about/over 90%' perform at least two tasks counts all non-candidate heads, including Table 3's 5.5% 'minor exception' and 2.7% bisemantic. Table 3 lists 81.9% as strictly polysemantic.

statements.problem: None. 14/144 = 9.7% (Table 3). Section 4.1.1 says about 90% and Appendix J says over 90% perform at least two tasks. Appendix J.1 calls the results a lower bound on polysemantic heads.
